claims.statement: MLPerf Tiny v0.5 specifies four benchmarks (keyword spotting, visual wake words, image classification, anomaly detection), each with a dataset, a model and a quality target (90% Top-1, 80% Top-1, 85% Top-1, AUC 0.85), and measures accuracy, latency and energy.
confidence_reasons: design facts stated by the authors and consistent between Table 1 and section 4

claims.statement: TFLite model sizes are 52.5 KB (keyword spotting DS-CNN, 38.6K parameters), 325 KB (visual wake words MobileNetV1), 96 KB (image classification ResNet) and 270 KB (anomaly detection autoencoder).
confidence_reasons: values in Table 1 and section 4 agree

claims.statement: Datasets and preprocessing: Speech Commands v2 reduced to 12 classes; MSCOCO 2014 reduced to person/no-person with a 2.5% area threshold at 96x96; CIFAR-10 at 32x32x3; DCASE2020 Toy-car with seven cars of 1000 normal samples each for training.

Reference quality figures reported by the authors: keyword spotting quantized model 91.6% (full test set) and 91.7% (1000-utterance subset), 92.2% in their experiments; visual wake words about 86%; image classification 86.5% on 200 images; anomaly detection AUC 0.88 (fp32) and 0.86 (quantized) on 248 samples.
claims.scope: reference models on stated test sets

claims.statement: Quality targets sit below the reference figures: about 6 points for visual wake words (about 86% vs 80%), 1.5 for image classification (86.5% vs 85%), 1.6 for keyword spotting (91.6% vs 90%) and 0.01 AUC for anomaly detection (0.86 quantized vs 0.85); the authors state that targets allow for quantization and rounding differences.

The measurement window covers model inference only (no pre- or post-processing). Latency score is the median inferences per second of five runs of at least 10 s and 10 iterations; energy is micro-Joules per inference with the same median-of-five rule; accuracy comes from one pass over the whole validation set and a minimum accuracy makes a score valid.
confidence_reasons: procedure stated twice (main text and appendix) consistently

claims.statement: Closed division: same model, dataset and quality target as the reference, post-training quantization allowed, no retraining; open division: submitter may change model, training scripts and dataset, need not meet the accuracy threshold and must document deviations; modifying orange components of the reference forces open division.

The benchmark framework couples a host PC runner to the device under test over a serial port; an energy configuration adds an isolating IO Manager and one of three supported energy monitors, excludes level-shifter power, and allows only one power supply for the core.

The authors state that CoreMark does not profile full programs or represent ML inference, that MLMark uses models too large for MCU-class devices and lacks power measurement, and that the MLPerf inference suite excludes MCUs for lack of small benchmarks; on that basis they describe MLPerf Tiny as the first industry-standard TinyML suite.
confidence_reasons: authors' own account of related work
cited sources read at abstract level only
claims.scope: three benchmarks named by the authors

claims.statement: The first submission round (June 2021) produced results in both divisions from an ARM MCU baseline, a RISC-V MCU, a Raspberry Pi 4 running a software toolchain, a neural-network accelerator and an FPGA flow (Table 2 lists five rows).
confidence_reasons: numeric results not in the paper text

claims.statement: Across the first-round submissions, 8-bit integer was the most common numerical format, frameworks ranged from open-source interpreters to hardware-specific compilers, platforms included MCUs, accelerators and FPGAs, and power consumption ranged from microWatts to Watts.
None of the first-round submissions modified the training dataset.

The authors report that the four reference implementations, run on the NUCLEO-L4R5ZI board, span a wide range of latency and energy and each meets its minimum accuracy; the latency and energy values are shown only in a figure whose data are not in the evidence.

The authors attribute the diversity of first-round submissions to the modular design (swappable reference components plus closed and open divisions); the evidence is consistent with this but no comparison design isolates the cause.
The authors expect modification of the training dataset to become more common in future rounds, in line with a wider shift towards data-centric design.

Leaving feature extraction outside the measurement while letting submitters choose it creates a possible degenerate case in which all layers but the last are called feature extraction; including it, one second of audio would mean one inference cycle and 40 feature extraction cycles, which would over-emphasize its cost; the authors therefore list the choice as an unresolved tradeoff.
confidence_reasons: reasoning stated by authors; not tested

claims.statement: The authors present the performance versus energy tradeoff, set by supply voltage and on-board power conversion efficiency, as a key insight of the benchmark and expose voltage selection in the runner.
confidence_reasons: assertion without data in the text

claims.statement: Future versions may add application domains (wearables, medical devices, environmental monitoring), more layer types such as RNNs, pre-processing in the measured scope, and a long-term stable subset.

The authors report that the benchmarks have been used as a standard set of tasks in TinyML research and as public projects on a TinyML development platform; the repository README lists further releases (v0.7, v1.0, v1.1 with release dates) and an expected v1.2 deadline.
Submissions are peer-reviewed transparently by the group of submitters and a review committee, are accepted twice a year, and each is public with reproduction instructions.

limitations.statement: Per-benchmark latency and energy values of the reference implementations and per-submission results are not available in the paper text used as evidence (they appear only in Figure 5 and on an external results site).
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Claims about the range of latency and energy are qualitative only.
limitations.resolution: Supply Figure 5 data or the results repository.

limitations.statement: Accuracy targets are validated on subsets (200 images, 1000 utterances, 248 samples) with no spread or repeat count.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Margins between reference values and targets cannot be judged against evaluation noise.

limitations.statement: Streaming inputs are not represented and feature extraction is excluded from measurement.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Measured latency and energy cover the model only, not a full audio pipeline.
limitations.resolution: Authors aim to widen scope to pre-processing in future versions.

limitations.statement: Closed-division models are mainly fully connected and convolutional networks.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Results do not speak to recurrent or other architectures.

limitations.statement: Insights rest on one submission round from a self-selected set of submitters.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Trends are a snapshot; the paper itself calls them a snapshot.

limitations.statement: Tension between adding benchmarks and keeping the suite stable for historical comparison is unresolved.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Long-term comparability is a plan, not a demonstrated property.

limitations.statement: The claim that energy-monitor sampling frequency does not affect the score, and the voltage-tradeoff insight, are stated without supporting measurements.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: Energy methodology is described, not validated in the paper text.

limitations.statement: The comparison with existing benchmarks is the authors' account and the cited works were not read in this process.
limitations.effect_on_interpretation: The novelty framing is attributed, not independently checked.

negative_result_decisions.reason: bears on the interpretation of submission diversity
